strengths: The paper addresses an identifiable audience in high-dimensional classification and factor models. Studying whitening and feature selection under diverging covariance spikes is a useful research direction.

The distinction between sparsity of the discriminant direction and sparsity of whitened mean differences is explained clearly. Entrywise eigenspace perturbation bounds provide a well-motivated approach to analyzing the latter.
The experimental design includes relevant baselines, 200 Monte Carlo replications with standard deviations, two real datasets, and a matched-sparsity sensitivity experiment.
weaknesses: Necessary: The QDA reduction in Eq. (5.5) is false under the stated assumptions, invalidating the Bayes-optimality claim in Theorem 6. Sparse whitened means do not imply that covariance information outside their support can be discarded. For example, take equal priors, u=(0,1,...,1)/sqrt(p−1), μ1=e1, μ2=2e1, Σ1=I+p uuᵀ, and Σ2=I+4p uuᵀ. These satisfy the spiked-covariance, coherence, and sparse-whitened-mean conditions. Both whitened means are supported on {1}, so the population projected classifier uses only Z1 and has optimal error Φ(−1/2). However, uᵀZ supplies additional variance information, giving the full Bayes classifier strictly lower limiting error. The extension requires additional structural restrictions, a different selection rule, or removal of the claim.

Necessary: The proof does not establish Theorem 3 as stated. The theorem asserts almost-sure convergence of conditional classification risk under log p=o(n), whereas Section 8.4 concludes joint convergence in probability of discriminant scores under the stronger condition (log n)(log p)=o(n). Joint convergence in probability does not establish almost-sure convergence of conditional risk. Supply the missing argument under the advertised assumptions or narrow the theorem and corresponding claims.

Necessary: The simulation results contain discrepancies that undermine their reliability. For Model 2 as specified, the squared Mahalanobis separation is [10−100ρ/(1+19ρ)]/(1−ρ). Thus, at ρ=0.9, the Bayes error is approximately 0.0196%, whereas Table 3 reports an oracle error of 5.40%. This cannot reasonably be explained by the stated Monte Carlo variability. Table 1 also repeats several means and standard deviations between ρ=0.7 and 0.8, including the oracle, despite different theoretical errors. Audit the implementation and table assembly, and correct the accompanying claims of highest accuracy.

Necessary: Section 7.3 overstates the elliptical extension. For a common non-Gaussian radial density h and unequal class priors, the Bayes rule compares log h(r1²)−log h(r2²) with a prior-dependent threshold; it generally does not reduce to Gaussian Fisher LDA. Sub-Gaussian tails do not resolve this mismatch. Restrict the claim to conditions that justify the decision rule, such as equal priors and a common decreasing radial density, or derive the appropriate classifier.

Necessary: Resolve the whitening-estimator definition. Section 2.3 defines Λ̂ as the leading eigenvalues of the sample covariance, which estimate λk+σ², but then constructs D̂=(Λ̂+σ̂²I)^(−1/2), adding the bulk variance again. Clarify whether Λ̂ contains full eigenvalues or estimated spike increments, and make the algorithm, perturbation identities, and experimental implementation consistent.

Necessary: Align the advertised scope with the analysis. The abstract presents a sparsity-dependent consistency condition, but Assumption 2 and Remark 1 explicitly fix the support size and leave growing sparsity unproved. The practical 90%-variance rank selection and cross-validated support selection also differ from the procedures covered by the consistency arguments. Clearly delimit which guarantees apply to which procedure.

Optional: Runtime and memory measurements, together with repeated real-data splits, would improve the practical assessment. The rejection is driven by substantive correctness and evidence failures in the supplied manuscript.
